---
<!-- quest-1: body_md -->
\label{q:doesTPimplySCH}
	Is it consistent for SCH to fail above a cardinal with the strong tree property?
<!-- end quest-1 -->
<!-- quest-2: body_md -->
Assuming the strong tree property, do all $(\kappa,\lambda)$-trees generated from narrow concrete $(\kappa,\lambda)$-systems have a cofinal branch?
<!-- end quest-2 -->
<!-- quest-3: body_md -->
Which trees admit narrow subsystems?
<!-- end quest-3 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
A partial order $(T, \leq_T)$ is a \emph{tree} if it has a minimal element (known as the root), and for all $y\in T$, the set $\operatorname{Pred}(y) = \{x\in T \mid x\leq_T y\}$ is well-ordered.
	
	The \emph{height} of an element $x\in T$ is $\operatorname{ht}(x) = \operatorname{ot}(\operatorname{Pred}(x))$. The \emph{$\alpha$-th level} of $T$ is $T_\alpha = \{x\in T \mid \operatorname{ht}(x) = \alpha\}$. The \emph{height} of a tree $T$ is $\sup_{x\in T}(\operatorname{ht}(x)+1)$.
	
	We say that a tree of height $\kappa$ is \emph{thin} if all levels have size $<\kappa$.
	
	The \emph{cone} above a node $x$ is $C(x) = \{y\in T \mid x\leq_T y\}$. If $x$ appears in multiple trees, we will sometimes write this as $C_T(x)$ to clarify which tree we are drawing elements from.
	
	We say that a cone $C$ above a node $x \in T_\alpha$ is \emph{unbounded} if $C(x)\cap T_\beta$ is nonempty for all $\beta >\alpha$.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
Let $I \subseteq \kappa$ be unbounded. A sequence $S = \langle S_\alpha \mid \alpha \in I \rangle$, equipped with a partial order $\leq_S$ on $\bigcup_{\alpha\in I} S_\alpha$, is a \emph{system of one relation} with height $\kappa$ and index set $I$ if the following hold:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $\alpha,\beta \in I$. Let $x \in S_\alpha$ and $y \in S_\beta$. If $x \leq_S y$, then either $\alpha <\beta$ or $\alpha = \beta$ and $x=y$.
		\item Let $\alpha_0$ and $\alpha_1$ both be below $\beta$. Then $x_0 \in S_{\alpha_0}$, $x_1 \in S_{\alpha_1}$ and $y\in S_\beta$, $x_0$ and $x_1$ are comparable.
		\item For all $\alpha < \beta$ both in $I$, there exists $x \in S_\alpha$ and $y\in S_\beta$ such that $x \leq_S y$.
	\end{enumerate}

	We will abuse notation and use $S$ to refer to both the system itself and the set $\bigcup_{\alpha\in I} S_\alpha$.
	
	The \emph{width} of a system is $\operatorname{width}(S) = \sup_{\alpha\in I}(|S_\alpha|)$. A system is \emph{thin} if $|S_\alpha|<\kappa$ for all $\alpha \in I$, and \emph{narrow} if $\operatorname{width}(S)^+ < \kappa$.
	
	A \emph{cofinal branch} through $S$ is a set $b = \{x_\alpha \mid \alpha \in I\}$ such that each $x_\alpha \in S_\alpha$, and for all $\alpha < \beta$ both in $I$, $x_\alpha \leq_S x_\beta$.
	
	The \emph{narrow system property} holds at $\kappa$ if every narrow system of height $\kappa$ with one relation has a cofinal branch.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
For both systems and trees, by enumerating the levels $T_\alpha$ and $S_\alpha$, we can assume that the $\zeta$-th element of the $\alpha$-th level is of the form $(\alpha, \zeta)$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
Let $(T, \leq_T)$ be a tree of height $\kappa$. We say that a system $S$ is a subsystem of $T$ if each $S_\alpha \subseteq T_\alpha$, and $\leq_S = \leq_T\upharpoonright \bigcup_{\alpha < \kappa} S_\alpha$.
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
Let $\kappa$ be regular. A \emph{concrete $\kappa$-system} is a sequence $S = \langle S_\alpha \mid \alpha \in I\rangle$ such that:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $I$ is a cofinal subset of $\kappa$.
		\item For all $\alpha \in I$, $S_\alpha$ is a nonempty collection of subsets of $\alpha$.
		\item For all $\alpha \leq \beta$ both in $I$, there is $y\in S_\beta$ such that $y\cap \alpha \in S_\alpha$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
Let $S$ be a concrete $\kappa$-system. The \emph{tree generated from $S$} is the tree $T$ whose levels are defined in the following way. The $\alpha$-th level of $T$ consists of $\{(\alpha,x\cap \alpha) \mid x\in S_\beta \text{ for some } \beta \geq \alpha\}$. If $(\alpha, x) \in T_\alpha$ and $(\beta, y) \in T_\beta$, then $(\alpha,x)\leq_T (\beta,y)$ if and only if $\beta \geq \alpha$ and $x = y\cap \alpha$.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- quest-4: body_md -->
Which trees (up to isomorphism) can be generated by narrow concrete $\kappa$-systems?
<!-- end quest-4 -->
<!-- exmp-1: body_md -->
Partition $\kappa$ into two unbounded sets, $A_0$ and $A_1$. Let $I = \{\alpha+1 \mid \alpha \in A_1\}$. Further partition $A_1$ into $\kappa$-many unbounded sets $B_\alpha$. Let $x^0_{\alpha+1} = A_0\cap (\alpha+1)$. Let $x^1_{\alpha+1} = B_\beta\cap (\alpha+1)$, where $\beta$ is the unique ordinal such that $\alpha \in B_\beta$.
	
	We define a concrete $\kappa$-system $S = \langle \{x^0_\alpha, x^1_\alpha\} \mid \alpha \in I\rangle$. This is a concrete system with width $2$, since the coherence requirement is satisfied by the $x_\alpha^0$'s.
	
	Despite $S$ having such small width, the tree it generates is not thin. The tree generated from $S$ consists of one branch of height $\kappa$ whose elements are initial segments of $A_0$, along with a branch of height $\alpha$ extending from the root for each $\alpha$ in the index set $I$ whose elements are initial segments of the $B_{\beta}$'s. Each level has size $\kappa$, even though the original system only had width $2$.
<!-- end exmp-1 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
Let $\kappa$ be a regular uncountable cardinal, with $\kappa \leq \lambda$. A \emph{$(\kappa, \lambda)$-tree} is a sequence $T = \langle T_z \mid z\in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)\rangle$ with the following properties:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item For all $z \in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$, $T_z$ is a nonempty collection of subsets of $z$.
		\item If $z \subseteq y$ are both in $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$, then for all $x \in T_y$, $x\cap z \in T_z$.
	\end{itemize}
	The entries $T_z$ are called the \emph{levels} of $T$. There is a natural tree-like order $\leq_T$ given by this structure: if $z \subseteq z'$ and $x\in T_z$, $y\in T_{z'}$, then $x \leq_T y$ iff $y\cap z = x$.
	
	A $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree is \emph{thin} if $|T_z|<\kappa$ for all $z\in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$.
	
	A \emph{cofinal branch} through $T$ is a subset $b\subseteq \lambda$ such that $b\cap z \in T_z$ for all $z\in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$.
	
	The \emph{strong tree property}\footnote{Many papers on the strong tree property, including several written by the author, define it in terms of different objects, called thin $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$ lists, rather than thin $(\kappa,\lambda)$-trees. The two definitions are equivalent.} holds at $\kappa$ if for all $\lambda \geq \kappa$ and all thin $(\kappa,\lambda)$-trees $T$, there is a cofinal branch through $T$.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
\cite[Definition 2.1]{lambie-hanson:narrowsystems}
	Let $\kappa$ be a regular uncountable cardinal, and let $\lambda \geq \kappa$. A concrete $\mathcal{P}(\kappa,\lambda)$-system is a sequence $S = \langle S_z\mid z\in I\rangle$ such that:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $I$ is a $\subseteq$-cofinal subset of $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$.
		\item For all $z\in I$, $S_z$ is a nonempty collection of subsets of $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$.
		\item For all $z \subseteq z'$ both in $I$, there is $y \in S_{z'}$ such that $y\cap z \in S_z$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	The \emph{width} of $S$ is $\operatorname{width}(S) = \sup_{x\in I} |S_x|$. $S$ is \emph{narrow} if $\operatorname{width}(S)^+<\kappa$. A \emph{cofinal branch} through $S$ is a set $b\subseteq \lambda$ such that $\{b\cap z \in S_z\}$ is $\subseteq$-unbounded in $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
Suppose $S = \langle S_z \mid z \in I\rangle$ is a concrete $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$-system. We define the \emph{$(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree $T$ generated from $S$} as follows. For all $x\in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$, we set $T_x = \{y\cap x \mid \exists z\in I, z\supseteq x \text{ and } y\in S_z\}$.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:LH}
	Let $\kappa$ be regular. Suppose that for all $\lambda \geq \kappa$ and all concrete narrow $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$-systems $S$, the $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree generated by $S$ has a cofinal branch. Then SCH holds above $\kappa$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- quest-5: body_md -->
Does the strong tree property at $\kappa$ imply the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{thm:LH}?
<!-- end quest-5 -->
<!-- quest-6: body_md -->
Do all $(\kappa,\lambda)$-trees generated from narrow systems contain a thin subtree?
<!-- end quest-6 -->
<!-- defn-9: body_md -->
The \emph{fan of height $\kappa$} is the tree consisting of $\kappa$-many separate branches extending from the root node, with the $\alpha$-th branch having height $\alpha$.
<!-- end defn-9 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:1-fan}
	If $\kappa$ is regular, a fan of height $\kappa$ has no narrow (or even thin) subsystem.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $T$ be the fan of height $\kappa$. Suppose that $S$ is a thin subsystem of $T$, with index set $I$. Consider $S_\alpha$ for some $\alpha \in I$ with $\alpha>0$. For all $\beta \in I$ with $\alpha < \beta$, there must be some $x_\beta \in S_\alpha$ and $y_\beta \in S_\beta$ such that $x_\beta \leq_S y_\beta$.
	
	Since $S$ is thin, $\{x_\beta \mid \beta \in I\setminus\alpha\}$ has size $<\kappa$. Then there is some $x\in S_\alpha$ such that $x = x_\beta$ for unboundedly many $\beta$. This means that $x$ has unboundedly many nodes above it in $S$ and thus in $T$. But no node in $T$ other than the root satisfies this property, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defn-10: body_md -->
Fix $\kappa$ regular, and let $T$ be a tree of height $\kappa$. We define the property \emph{$\alpha$-fanlike} for cones in $T$ inductively as follows.
	\begin{itemize}
	\item A cone is $0$-fanlike if it is bounded.
	
	\item A cone $C$ above a node $x$ on level $\beta$ is $(\alpha+1)$-fanlike if there is $\delta$ with $\beta \leq \delta < \kappa$ such that for each node $y \in T_\delta\cap C$, the cone above $y$ is $\alpha$-fanlike.
	
	\item If $\gamma$ is a limit ordinal, a cone $C$ above a node $x$ on level $\beta$ is $\gamma$-fanlike if there is $\delta$ with $\beta \leq \delta < \kappa$ such that for all $y \in T_\delta\cap C$, the cone above $y$ is $\alpha$-fanlike for some $\alpha < \gamma$.
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-10 -->
<!-- defn-11: body_md -->
We say that a tree $T$ of height $\kappa$ with root $r$ is \emph{$\alpha$-fanlike} if $C_T(r)$ is $\alpha$-fanlike. That is, if $T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike when we view it as the cone above the root. $T$ is \emph{fanlike} if it is $\alpha$-fanlike for any $\alpha$.
<!-- end defn-11 -->
<!-- defn-12: body_md -->
Let $\kappa$ regular, and let $T$ be a tree of height $\kappa$. We say that $T$ is \emph{fanlike} if $T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike for some ordinal $\alpha$. The \emph{fan degree} of a fanlike tree $T$, written $\operatorname{fd}(T)$, is the least $\alpha$ such that $T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike.
<!-- end defn-12 -->
<!-- defn-13: body_md -->
A tree $T$ is well-pruned if every node extends to an element on every higher level.
<!-- end defn-13 -->
<!-- defn-14: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a tree of height $\kappa$. We define the $\alpha$-th prune of $T$, written $T^\alpha$, inductively. Let $T^0 = T$. At successor stages $\alpha$, we define $B_\alpha = \{x \mid C_{T^\alpha}(x) \text{ is bounded}\}$, and let $T^{\alpha+1} = T\setminus \bigcup_{x\in B_0}C_T(x)$. That is, we ``prune'' $T_\alpha$ by removing all nodes that have bounded cones. At limit stages, we define $T^\gamma = \bigcap_{\alpha<\gamma} T^\alpha$.
<!-- end defn-14 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
Note that if $T$ is well-pruned, then this process does nothing: $B_\alpha$ will be empty for all $\alpha$.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:pruningsurvivors}
	Let $x \in T$. Then $x\in T^{\alpha}$ if and only if $C_T(x)$ is not $\beta$-fanlike (in $T$) for any $\beta < \alpha$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We prove this by induction on $\alpha$. 
	Our base case is $\alpha = 1.$ By definition, $x \in T^1$ if and only if $C_{T^0}(x) = C_T(x)$ is not bounded, which by definition holds if and only if $C_T(x)$ is not $0$-fanlike.
	
	Next, the successor stage. It suffices to show that $x \in T^{\alpha+1}$ if and only if $C_T(x)$ is not $\alpha$-fanlike. By definition, $x \in T^{\alpha+1}$ if and only if $C_{T^\alpha}(x)$ is unbounded. Applying our inductive hypothesis, for all $y \in T^{\alpha}$, $C_T(y)$ is not $\beta$-fanlike for any $\beta < \alpha$. We conclude that $C_{T^\alpha}(x)$ is unbounded if and only if all levels in $C_T(x)$ above the level of $x$ contain some element $y$ such that $C_T(y)$ is not $\beta$-fanlike for any $\beta < \alpha$. This occurs if and only if $C_T(x)$ is not $\alpha$-fanlike.
	
	Finally, let $\gamma$ be a limit ordinal. Then $x\in T^\gamma$ if and only if $x \in T^\alpha$ for all $\alpha < \gamma$, so by our inductive hypothesis $x\in T^\gamma$ if and only if $C_T(x)$ is not $\beta$-fanlike for any $\beta < \gamma$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:flpruning}
	$T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike if and only if $T^{\alpha+1}$ is empty.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose $T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike. Let $x$ be the root of $T$. Then $C_T(x) = T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike, so by Lemma \ref{lem:pruningsurvivors}, $x$ is not in $T^{\alpha+1}$. Since $x$ is the root of $T$, it will only be missing from $T^{\alpha+1}$ if $T^{\alpha+1}$ is empty.
	
	Suppose $T$ is not $\alpha$-fanlike. Let $x$ be the root of $T$. Then $C_T(x) = T$ is not $\alpha$-fanlike, so $x\in T^{\alpha+1}$, and thus $T^{\alpha+1}$ is not empty.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:pruningstabilizes}
	There is an ordinal $\beta < |T|^+$ such that for all $\beta' > \beta$, $T^{\beta'} = T^\beta$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First, note that if $T^\beta = T^{\beta+1}$, then $T^\beta$ has no elements with bounded cones, so $T^{\beta'} = T^\beta$ for all $\beta' >\beta$. That is, if the sequence is constant for even two consecutive elements, it must stabilize completely.
	
	Suppose the pruning does not stabilize at stage $\alpha$, so $T_{\alpha+1}\neq T_\alpha$. Then $T_{\alpha+1}$ is a proper subset of $T_\alpha$, and thus we have removed at least one node. If the process never stabilizes before stage $|T|^+$, then we will have removed $|T|^+$-many nodes from $T$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:FLiffWPsubtree}
	A tree $T$ has a well-pruned subtree if and only if it is not fanlike.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Suppose $T$ has a well pruned subtree $T'$. Then $T' \subseteq T^\alpha$ for all $\alpha$: no nodes of $T'$ can be removed at successor stages, because all nodes in $T'$ have unbounded cones in $T'$. At limits we take intersections, so all of $T'$ will also survive limit stages. We conclude that $T^{\alpha+1}$ is nonempty for all $\alpha$, so by Corollary \ref{cor:flpruning}, $T$ cannot be $\alpha$-fanlike for any $\alpha$.
	 
	 Now suppose $T$ is not fanlike. Then it is not $\alpha$-fanlike for any $\alpha$, so by Corollary \ref{cor:flpruning}, $T^\alpha$ is nonempty for all $\alpha$. By Lemma \ref{lem:pruningstabilizes}, the $T^\alpha$'s stabilize at some stage $\beta < |T|^+$. Define $T' = T^\beta$. Since $T^\beta = T^{\beta+1}$ and $T^\beta$ is nonempty, we conclude that all nodes in $T^\beta$ have unbounded cones, and thus $T^\beta$ is a well-pruned subtree of $T$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:1cardmain}
	Let $\kappa$ be regular. Suppose $T$ is a tree of height $\kappa$ that admits a narrow system. Then $T$ contains a well-pruned subtree.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose $T$ does not have a well-pruned subtree, but does have a narrow subsystem $S = \langle S_\alpha \mid \alpha \in I \rangle$. Let $\theta = \operatorname{width}(S)$, noting that $\theta^+ < \kappa$.
	
	We will prove something slightly stronger than the statement of the theorem. Given $\alpha \in I$, we say that a subset $C\subseteq T$ \emph{hits $\alpha$} if $C\cap S_\alpha$ is nonempty. We claim that there is some $\alpha < \kappa$ such that for any selection $A$ of $\leq \theta$-many nodes in $T_\alpha$, the cone above $A$, written $C(A) = \bigcup_{x\in A}C(x)$, misses unboundedly many elements of $I$. In particular, this means that the coherence requirement of the system $S$ must fail: if we set $A = S_\alpha$, then there will be some $\gamma > \alpha$ such that nothing in $S_\gamma$ is above anything in $S_\alpha$.
	
	Suppose that the claim fails for $T$. This means that for all $\alpha < \kappa$, there is a set $A_\alpha$  of $\leq\theta$-many nodes in $T_\alpha$ and an ordinal $\gamma_\alpha$ such that $A_\alpha$ hits all levels $\geq \gamma_\alpha$.
	
	Since $T$ has no well-pruned subtree, by Lemma \ref{lem:FLiffWPsubtree} it is $\rho$-fanlike for some ordinal $\rho$.	This means that there is some $\delta$ such that the cones above every node in $T_\delta$ are $\rho'$-fanlike for some $\rho'<\rho$. Set $\alpha_0 = \delta$.
	
	For each element $x\in A_{\alpha_0}$, since $C(x)$ is fanlike, there is some $\delta_x$ such that for all $y \in C(x)$ with $\operatorname{Lev}(y) \geq \delta_x$, $\operatorname{fd}(C(y)) < \operatorname{fd}(C(x))$. Let $\alpha_1 = \sup_{x\in A_{\alpha_0}}\delta_x$.
	
	We repeat this process inductively, taking supremums at limit stages, defining an increasing sequence $\langle \alpha_\beta \mid \beta < \theta^+\rangle$ such that for all $x \in A_{\alpha_\beta}$ and all $y \in C_x$ at or above level $\alpha_{\beta+1}$, $\operatorname{fd}(C(y))<\operatorname{fd}(C(x))$.
	
	\begin{claim}\label{cl:wellfounded}
		For any $x$ in any $C(A_{\alpha_\beta})$, $B_x = \{\beta' \mid x\in C(A_{\alpha_{\beta'}})\}$ is finite.
	\end{claim}
	\begin{proof}
		Suppose $\langle \beta_n \mid n<\omega\rangle$ is an increasing sequence of elements in $\theta^+$, and suppose $x \in \bigcap_{n<\omega}C(A_{\alpha_{\beta_n}})$. Then there is a  sequence $x_n$ such that each $x_n \in A_{\alpha_{\beta_n}}$, and $x \in C(x_n)$. Since $T$ is a tree, all nodes in this this sequence must be comparable; since their levels are increasing, the sequence is $\leq_T$-increasing.
		
		For all $n<m<\omega$, since $x_n \leq_T x_m$ and $x_m$ is above level $\alpha_{\beta_n}$, by construction $\operatorname{fd}(C(x_m)) < \operatorname{fd}(C(x_n))$.
		This gives an infinite decreasing sequence of ordinals, a contradiction.
	\end{proof}
	
	Let $\gamma = \sup_{\beta < \theta^+}\gamma_\beta$. Then for all $\beta < \theta^+$, $C(A_{\alpha_\beta})\cap S_\gamma$ must be nonempty.
	For all $y \in S_\gamma$, consider the set $B_y = \{\beta <\theta^+ \mid y\in C(A_{\alpha_\beta})\}$. Clearly $\bigcup_{y\in S_\gamma} B_y = \theta^+$, since each $C(A_{\alpha_\beta})$ intersects $S_\gamma$. Since $S_\gamma$ has size at most $\theta$, there is some $y \in S_\gamma$ such that $B_y$ has size $\theta^+$.
	This means that $y$ is in $C(A_{\alpha_\beta})$ for infinitely many $\beta$, contradicting Claim \ref{cl:wellfounded}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
\label{cl:wellfounded}
		For any $x$ in any $C(A_{\alpha_\beta})$, $B_x = \{\beta' \mid x\in C(A_{\alpha_{\beta'}})\}$ is finite.
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Suppose $\langle \beta_n \mid n<\omega\rangle$ is an increasing sequence of elements in $\theta^+$, and suppose $x \in \bigcap_{n<\omega}C(A_{\alpha_{\beta_n}})$. Then there is a  sequence $x_n$ such that each $x_n \in A_{\alpha_{\beta_n}}$, and $x \in C(x_n)$. Since $T$ is a tree, all nodes in this this sequence must be comparable; since their levels are increasing, the sequence is $\leq_T$-increasing.
		
		For all $n<m<\omega$, since $x_n \leq_T x_m$ and $x_m$ is above level $\alpha_{\beta_n}$, by construction $\operatorname{fd}(C(x_m)) < \operatorname{fd}(C(x_n))$.
		This gives an infinite decreasing sequence of ordinals, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- exmp-2: body_md -->
Recall that when we defined the $\omega$-fan, our procedure at limits was aimed at preserving the properties of the $n$-fans. But we could have iterated the construction in a different way. That is, if we view each $n+1$-fan $F_{n+1}$ as extending a $n$-fan $F_n$ by adding a $1$-fan to the end of each branch, we can define a tree $F = \bigcup_{n<\omega} F_n$. (In fact, we can continue this process transfinitely, as long as we stop at a limit stage below stage $\kappa$; for simplicity, we will stop at stage $\omega$.) This should be thought of as iterating the process of adding a $1$-fan to the end of each branch $\omega$-many times.

	The tree $F$ has some interesting properties. First, unlike the fanlike trees described in the previous section, it is well-pruned. It is also highly homogeneous: for any node $x$, $C(x)$ is isomorphic to the full tree. It has no cofinal branches, since each branch consists of concatenating countably many segments each of which has length $<\kappa$. Moreover this remains true in any extension in which $\kappa$ remains a regular cardinal. Finally, we note that $F$ contains no thin subtree of height $\kappa$.
<!-- end exmp-2 -->
<!-- exmp-3: body_md -->
A well-known theorem due to Specker \cite{specker}, generalizing the standard construction of an special Aronszajn tree, states that if $\kappa^{<\kappa} = \kappa$, then there is a $\kappa^+$-Aronszajn tree. A proof of his theorem using walks on ordinals appears in \cite{kanamori}. The cardinal arithmetic assumption is only used to show that the levels are thin; if it fails, the tree can still be constructed, and is a wide $\kappa^+$-Aronszajn tree that is well-pruned. In particular, if the tree property holds at $\kappa^+$, then the tree built in this manner will be wide.
<!-- end exmp-3 -->
<!-- defn-15: body_md -->
A $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree $T$ is \emph{well-pruned} if for every element $x \in T_z$ and all $z' \supseteq z$, there is $y\in T_{z'}$ such that $y\cap z = x$. That is, every node in $T$ has an extension to all larger levels.
<!-- end defn-15 -->
<!-- defn-16: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree, and let $C$ be a cone in $T$. We define the notion of \emph{$\alpha$-fanlike} inductively:
	\begin{itemize}
	\item A cone $C$ in $T$ is $0$-fanlike if it is bounded.
	
	\item A cone $C$ above a node $x \in T_{z_0}$ is $\alpha+1$-fanlike if there is $z\in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$ with $z\supseteq z_0$ such that for each $y\in C\cap T_z$, the cone above $y$ is either bounded in $\mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$ or is $\alpha$-fanlike.
	
	\item If $\gamma$ is a limit ordinal, a cone $C$ above a node $x \in T_{z_0}$ is $\gamma$-fanlike if there is $z \in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$ with $z \supseteq z_0$ such that for all $y \in C\cap T_z$, the cone above $y$ is $\alpha$-fanlike for some $\alpha < \gamma$.
\end{itemize}
	
	We say that a $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree $T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike if the above definition holds, replacing $C$ with $T$.
<!-- end defn-16 -->
<!-- defn-17: body_md -->
Let $\kappa$ be regular, and let $T$ be a $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree. We say that $T$ is \emph{fanlike} if $T$ is $\alpha$-fanlike for some $\alpha$. The \emph{fan degree} of $T$ is the least such $\alpha$.
<!-- end defn-17 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:2cardfaniffwp}
	Let $\kappa$ be regular, and let $T$ be a $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree. Then $T$ has a well-pruned $(\kappa,\lambda)$-subtree if and only if $T$ is not fanlike.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Identical to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:FLiffWPsubtree}, noting that all lemmas used in that proof also generalize to $(\kappa,\lambda)$-trees with identical proofs.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
Let $\kappa$ be regular. Suppose $T$ is a $(\kappa,\lambda)$-tree that admits a narrow system. Then $T$ contains a well-pruned $(\kappa,\lambda)$-subtree.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Suppose $T$ does not have a well-pruned subtree, but contains a narrow subsystem $S = \langle S_z \mid z\in I$. Let $\theta = \operatorname{width}(S)$, with $\theta^+<\kappa$. 
	
	For $z\in I$, we say that a subset $C\subseteq T$ \emph{hits $z$} if $C\cap S_z$ is nonempty, and \emph{misses $z$} if the intersection is empty. As in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:1cardmain}, we will prove that there is some $z\in I$ such that for any selection $A$ of $\leq \theta$-many nodes in $T_z$, the union of the cones above elements of $A$ misses $\subseteq$-unboundedly many elements of $I$. As before, this will imply that $S$ cannot be a system.
		
	Suppose that this is not the case. Then for all $z\in I$, there is a set $A_z$ of $\leq \theta$-many nodes in $T_z$ and a set $g_z \in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$ such that $A_z$ hits $z'$ for all $z' \supseteq g_z$.
	
	Since $T$ has no well-pruned subtree, by Lemma \ref{lem:2cardfaniffwp} it is fanlike. Then there is $b\in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$ such that for all $x \in T_b$, $\operatorname{fd}(C(x)) < \operatorname{fd}(T)$. Set $a_0 = b$.
	
	For each element $x\in A_{a_0}$, since $C(x)$ is fanlike, there is $b_x$ such that for all $y \in C(x)\cap T_{b_x}$, $\operatorname{fd}(y) < \operatorname{fd}(x)$. Let $a_1 = \bigcup_{x\in A_{\alpha_0}} b_x$. Note that $A_{\alpha_0}$ has size $\leq \theta$, so $a_1 \in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$.
		
	We repeat this process $\theta^+$-many times, taking unions at limit stages, to define a $\subseteq$-increasing sequence $\langle a_\beta \mid \beta < \theta^+\rangle$ such that for all $x\in A_{a_\beta}$, $z\supseteq a_{\beta+1}$, and all $y\in C(x) \cap T_z$, $\operatorname{fd}(C(y)) < \operatorname{fd}(C(x))$.
	
	\begin{claim}
		For any $x$ in any $C(A_{a_\beta})$, $x$ appears in only finitely many cones $C(A_{a_{\beta'}})$.
	\end{claim}
	\begin{proof}
		Suppose that $\langle \beta_n \mid n<\omega\rangle$ is an increasing sequence of ordinals less than $\theta^+$ such that $x \in \bigcap_{n<\omega} C(A_{a_{\beta_n}})$. Then for all $n<\omega$, there is some $x_n$ such that $x_n \in A_{a_{\beta_n}}$ and $x\in C(x_n)$. The sequence $\langle x_n \mid n<\omega\rangle$ must be $\subseteq$-increasing, so in particular given $n<m$, $x_m \in C(x_m)$, above level $\beta_n$. We conclude that $\operatorname{fd}(x_m) < \operatorname{fd}(x_n)$ whenever $n<m$. This gives an infinite decreasing sequence of ordinals, a contradiction.
	\end{proof}
	
	Now let $g = \bigcup_{\beta < \theta^+} g_{a_\beta}$. Noting that $\theta^+<\kappa$, $g \in \mathcal{P}_\kappa(\lambda)$. Then for all $\beta < \theta^+$, $C(A_{a_\beta})\cap S_{g}$ is nonempty.
	For all $y \in S_{g}$, consider the set $B_y = \{\beta < \theta^+ \mid y\in C(A_{a_\beta})\}$. Since each $C(A_{a_\beta})$ hits $g$, $\bigcup_{\gamma\in S_\gamma}B_y  = \theta^+$. Since $S_{g}$ has size at most $\theta$, there is some $y\in S_\gamma$ such that $B_y$ has size $\theta^+$. This means that $y\in C(A_{a_\beta})$ for infinitely many $\beta$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
For any $x$ in any $C(A_{a_\beta})$, $x$ appears in only finitely many cones $C(A_{a_{\beta'}})$.
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Suppose that $\langle \beta_n \mid n<\omega\rangle$ is an increasing sequence of ordinals less than $\theta^+$ such that $x \in \bigcap_{n<\omega} C(A_{a_{\beta_n}})$. Then for all $n<\omega$, there is some $x_n$ such that $x_n \in A_{a_{\beta_n}}$ and $x\in C(x_n)$. The sequence $\langle x_n \mid n<\omega\rangle$ must be $\subseteq$-increasing, so in particular given $n<m$, $x_m \in C(x_m)$, above level $\beta_n$. We conclude that $\operatorname{fd}(x_m) < \operatorname{fd}(x_n)$ whenever $n<m$. This gives an infinite decreasing sequence of ordinals, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
